source.title: Natural Language Descriptions of Deep Visual Features
source.authors: Evan Hernandez; Sarah Schwettmann; David Bau; Teona Bagashvili; A. Torralba; Jacob Andreas

record.tranche_reason: The study uses neuron descriptions as a tool for visual-model analysis, auditing, and editing, but does not test the claim versions about pole-level job shares, explanations predicting new activations, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates MILAN against human descriptions and other labeling methods, but those results do not test the listed claim versions. It also reports neuron counts and interventions in applications; those are recorded below as findings about the claim's subject, but do not directly test a listed version. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: MILAN is a vision-neuron labelling tool. Its results score agreement with human captions and use the labels for ablation, auditing and editing. It never reports what share of neurons have one main job, in language models or elsewhere. It does not re-examine InceptionV1 mixed neurons, build neuron attribution graphs, or score explanations by predicting activations on new inputs. Its tool comparison (Table 2 BERTScore against NetDissect and Compositional Explanations) measures label agreement, not a share of interpretable neurons, so it does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MILAN automatically produces fine-grained natural-language neuron descriptions that agree with human annotations better than the baselines and support analysis, auditing and editing. They caution that the descriptions are partial, potentially noisy characterizations from a fixed set of representative inputs.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces MILAN, which searches for natural-language descriptions using a weighted pointwise-mutual-information objective and learned caption and language models; it does not use the pole-level audit method described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron ablation results vary with the caption-derived sorting criterion. In the text-feature editing experiment, the result differs between sorting text-selective neurons and sorting all neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet18-ImageNet, MILAN finds neurons described with dissimilar concepts (e.g. 'animals, vehicles, and vases'; 'dog faces and cupcakes'). Ablating them hurts accuracy less than random ablation. A cut-and-paste attack on one such neuron induces unrelated predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet ResNet18, neurons whose exemplar-based descriptions mix semantically dissimilar concepts are less important to accuracy and linked to non-robust predictions.

fits_no_version.finding: MILAN face-neuron counts fall in blurred-ImageNet models (142 vs 213 across models), but face-selective neurons remain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Face blurring in ImageNet training reduces but does not eliminate neurons labelled as selective for unblurred human faces.

fits_no_version.finding: In a ResNet18 trained with spurious text labels, ablating 13 MILAN-identified text neurons raises adversarial accuracy by 4.9 points; the sort-all comparator raises it by under 1 point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing description-selected spurious-feature neurons partly restores robustness in a vision classifier deliberately trained with a spurious text cue.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating neurons described with many adjectives or prepositions degrades ImageNet accuracy faster than random or noun-based ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet ResNet18, neurons whose descriptions emphasize attributes or relations are relatively important to accuracy.

record.problems: The authors describe MILAN descriptions as partial and potentially noisy, based on a fixed-sized set of representative inputs. The ablation-curve results in Figure 4 are not numerically reported in the text. The face-neuron counts are aggregate counts across models rather than per-model results. The spurious-text experiment intentionally induces the feature correlation.
record.rows_left_out: No listed-version result was omitted. The Section 4 generalization tables compare generated descriptions with human annotations using BERTScore, but do not test any listed version's pole-share or new-activation-prediction claim.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level shares (about 90% one job, about 7% two, 2–4% not understood).
Similar shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts, up to trillions of parameters. The study covers only vision CNNs and a ViT, and reports no shares.
Whether InceptionV1's cat-and-car-type neurons detect a coherent shared feature rather than superposition. MILAN's mixed-concept ResNet18 neurons are not analysed for a shared feature.
Share of interpretable neurons as a function of tools, architecture or regularization, including the 5% to 99% InceptionV1-sized estimates. No interpretable-neuron share is reported for any tool.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether exemplar-fitted explanations fail to predict where neurons fire on new inputs. The study only acknowledges exemplar-based explanations' known shortcomings in its impact statement.
Simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The study's subject is vision models (AlexNet, ResNet, BigGAN, DINO ViT, ResNet18), not language-model neuron poles. The BERTScore comparisons (Tables 2–3) are tool-versus-tool agreement with human labels. They are rightly left out of the rows as bearing on no version; in particular they are not an interpretable-neuron share for V4. This study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level job shares and the proportion of poles not understood.
Similar pole-level shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or very large scales.
Whether canonical InceptionV1 mixed-concept neurons detect a coherent shared feature rather than superposition.
The share of interpretable neurons as a function of tools, architecture, or model capacity, including the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Whether attribution graphs using a model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations matching activating examples fail to predict where neurons activate.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
